mathematical_statement: Task-sensitive candidate units do not possess dedicated circuit selectivity over activation-norm-matched random subsets at small k
empirical_metrics: Layer 1 k=8: Cand=0.340 vs NormRand=0.430 (Diff=-0.090 p_adj=1.0000) vs DimRand=0.120 (Diff=+0.220 p=1.23e-4). Layer 2 k=8: Cand=0.344 vs NormRand=0.283 (Diff=+0.061 p_raw=0.0368 p_adj=0.5155). Layer 2 k=32: Cand=0.823 vs NormRand=0.762 (Diff=+0.061 p_adj=0.0117). (N=60 pairs 482400 intervention records)
necessity_evidence: Condition-averaged ablation reduces contrast proportionally to subspace size
sufficiency_evidence: Candidate units maintain modest transfer advantage only at broad subspace sizes (k=32) but fail to beat norm-matched random controls in Layer 1 or at small k in Layer 2
specificity_controls: Activation-norm-matching (closest 100 of >=5000 draws within 5% tolerance) alongside unconstrained dimension-matched controls and Holm-Bonferroni correction over 20 tests
boundary_conditions: Falsifies the hypothesis that a small sparse subnetwork (k=8) forms an autonomous dedicated binding circuit. Layer 1 advantage is an activation-magnitude effect. Layer 2 advantage is distributed across the broad manifold
